posts.content:
We made an 1800s lighthouse lantern, and it works.

This is a functional 6th-order Fresnel lens replica, the smallest size used in real 19th and 20th century lighthouses. The entire design was 3D printed on the Formlabs Form 4 print ecosystem.

The lenses and catadioptric prisms are printed in Formlabs Clear V5. To get the optical clarity required to properly refract light, we wet-sanded every part to remove layer lines and finished them with a buffing process to achieve a glass-like finish.

The structural frame is printed in Formlabs Black V5, and the gears are printed in Tough 2000 V2, chosen for its high stiffness and creep resistance to support the weight of the solid resin lenses.

Everything is entirely custom-designed in CAD (Onshape). The refraction angles were manually calculated and ray traced for each individual prism so the light perfectly collimates into a horizontal beam.

Because a 6th-order lens is still quite large, the frame was designed to print in several pieces and assemble with dovetail joints.

It actually spins using a 12V DC gear motor with a 6:1 gear reduction system, rotating the lens at around 6 RPM on a lazy susan bearing. The mechanism is friction-driven, so the center of the base stays completely hollow, letting a stationary 12W dimmable vintage Edison bulb sit inside.

The lens takes the expanding light from the bulb and compresses it into a highly focused horizontal beam, creating that classic lighthouse "loom" sweeping across the room.

posts.content:
The rebound performance of flexible 3D printing resins keeps improving year after year.

If you’ve worked with flexible 3D printing materials for a while, you’ll probably remember when “flexible” often meant soft but not necessarily functional. Limited rebound, lower durability, and performance that was sometimes not even good enough for prototypes.

This is changing with the new Formlabs Flexible 80A Resin V2.

Compared to the previous version, it offers significant improvements across key mechanical properties:

- 4× higher rebound (13% → 56%)
- 2× higher tear strength (13 → 28 kN/m)
- 2× higher elongation at break (131% → 230%)
- 5× better fatigue resistance (Ross Flex Fatigue)

If you want to learn more about the material, feel free to write a comment or have a look at the following link: https://lnkd.in/eUKwmzSw

posts.content:
We printed this flexible football out of the all new Flexible 80A resin! 

This is how we did it - After printing on the Form 4L, we wash the build platform in IPA to remove any excess resin. We then remove the supports from the football and wash it again. After that we allow the football to dry completely overnight. We then submerge the football in water, and cure it using the the Form CureL for 5 minutes. For this print, we ended up flipping the ball halfway through to ensure an even cure. The ball was then cured again at 80C for 5 minutes, resulting in this final amazing ball. 

#3dprinting #football #formlabs

posts.content:
I first wrote about the Rule of 40 in 2015. It's now gospel in SaaS - growth plus profit should clear 40%.

People keep asking if it means anything for hardware. The answer is yes, but you can't read it the way you read SaaS.

A young hardware company doing everything right can fail the Rule of 40 for years. Tooling, supply chain, and manufacturing all cost real money up front, and margins show up late. The snapshot says "unhealthy." The company says "on track."

So don't read the snapshot. Read the curve. Is gross margin improving with each product generation? Is the company earning the right to turn on the profit engine? Formlabs looked bad early and great later. The difference was the slope.

https://lnkd.in/gqetRghn

posts.content:
One of the most common causes of print failures in SLS is foreign debris. A single hair can ruin a build and cost thousands of dollars in downtime. Print Intelligence eliminates this problem by detecting part defects in real time and selectively removing the affected part from the following layers. On another printer, a single hair could cause compounding defects that ruin an entire print. On Fuse X1, Print Intelligence isolates the failure and completes the rest of the build, maximizing part yield.

Read more here: https://lnkd.in/gGX7nPcC
